title: Perturb-and-Solve: Efficient Learned-Operator Conditioning for Latent Diffusion Inverse Problems

paper.title: Perturb-and-Solve: Efficient Learned-Operator Conditioning for Latent Diffusion Inverse Problems
paper.abstract:
Abstract Latent diffusion models serve as powerful priors for solving inverse problems
in image restoration, such as deblurring, inpainting, and super-resolution. Current methods have a trade-off between generality and efficiency. Solvers
that are restricted to a fixed set of degradation operators are fast and
efficient. Methods that support arbitrary degradation operators are slow and
require gradients through the diffusion network.
To break this bottleneck, we introduce PASEO ( P erturb- A nd- S olve for E fficient O perator conditioning), a method that uses a small
( ∼ \sim 1M parameters) learned network to degrade diffusion model predictions in latent space. PASEO supports learned degradation operators without back-propagating
through the diffusion network. We efficiently sample reconstructions from
an approximate posterior by combining the diffusion model’s prediction with the
observed image. We do this by adding noise and solving linear equations based
on a local linear approximation of the learned network, without building or
inverting large covariance matrices.
Across super-resolution, deblurring, and inpainting on FFHQ and COCO, PASEO achieves strong perceptual quality while running up to 19 × {\color[rgb]{0.2266,0.5586,0.7578}19\times} faster and
using up to 34 % {\color[rgb]{0.2266,0.5586,0.7578}34\%} less peak memory than the tested baselines, with the same or fewer
model evaluations.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: 𝐱 {\mathbf{x}} 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} PASEO (ours) SILO ReSample DAPS FlowChef FlowDPS Inpainting SR × 8 \times 8 Gaussian blur Figure 1: Visual comparison on COCO with SD3.5-medium prior. In image and signal processing, a signal of interest often cannot be observed directly and therefore must instead be recovered from indirect, incomplete or noisy measurements. This is known as an inverse problem , where we seek to recover an unknown signal 𝐱 {\mathbf{x}} from an indirect measurement 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} of that signal. The same measurement can come from different signals: for example, different sharp images can produce similar blurred observations. We therefore need additional information about what the original signal could be. The Bayesian formulation expresses this knowledge through a prior p ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) p({\mathbf{x}}) and uses a likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝐲 ∣ 𝐱 ) p({\mathbf{y}}\mid{\mathbf{x}}) to describe how a candidate signal could produce the observed measurement. Together, they define the posterior distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐱 ∣ 𝐲 ) ∝ p ⁡ ( 𝐲 ∣ 𝐱 ) ​ p ​ ( 𝐱 ) p({\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{y}})\propto p({\mathbf{y}}\mid{\mathbf{x}})p({\mathbf{x}}) , which describes plausible signals given the measurement. Inverse problems with diffusion models aim at generating plausible reconstructions through posterior sampling. For image reconstruction, the prior must capture the structure and detail of natural images, motivating the use of expressive generative models. Latent diffusion models (LDMs) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) provide effective image priors for inverse problems ( Rout et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Raphaeli et al., 2025 ) . They learn the structure and detail of natural images and generate images by working in a compact latent space. A pretrained autoencoder connects this space to images: its encoder maps an image to a latent representation, and its decoder maps that representation back to an image. Working in this smaller space reduces the cost of image generation. For image reconstruction, generating realistic images is not enough. The reconstructed image must also be similar to the measurement 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} . In the literature, this similarity is often called data consistency . Enforcing data consistency is harder with LDMs because the measurement 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} is in pixel space, while the model works in latent space. Many solvers therefore enforce data consistency by repeatedly running the encoder and decoder and back-propagating ( Rout et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Rout et al., 2024 ; Chung et al., 2024b ; Raphaeli et al., 2025 ) , increasing runtime and memory. Recent methods aim to improve reconstruction quality and reduce these costs. LD-SMC ( Achituve et al., 2025 ) and DDSMC ( Ekström Kelvinius et al., 2025 ) focus on more accurate posterior sampling, while SITCOM ( Alkhouri et al., 2025 ) , learnable linear extrapolation ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , SPIN ( Shtanchaev et al., 2026 ) , and CWGF ( Spagnoletti et al., 2026 ) create faster samplers. Other approaches use the structure of linear measurements, as in DMPS ( Meng & Kabashima, 2025 ) and pDDIM ( Jiao et al., 2026 ) ; modify the sampling procedure, as in DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) ; or extend reconstruction to flow-based generative models, as in PnP-Flow ( Martin et al., 2025 ) and FlowDPS ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . We build on the following two methods for reconstruction in latent space. DING ( Moufad et al., 2026 ) samples exactly from approximate posterior transitions without back-propagating through the denoising network. Its latent-space formulation is limited to inpainting, where a mask separates observed and missing regions and enables a simple exact sampling update. Other degradations generally require a different update. On the other hand, SILO ( Raphaeli et al., 2025 ) uses a small trained network to describe more general degradation processes in latent space. We denote this learned operator by 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} , where ψ \psi denotes its learned parameters. From a clean latent, the network predicts the encoding of the corresponding degraded image. This avoids repeatedly running the encoder and decoder during sampling, but SILO still back-propagates through the learned operator and the denoising network at every step to guide the reconstruction process. Our aim is to combine these benefits to support learned degradation operators in latent space while avoiding propagating gradients through the denoiser network. PASEO efficiently updates its estimate toward an approximate posterior by first forming a local linear approximation of the learned network 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} around the current clean-latent prior estimate obtained from the diffusion step. To avoid forming the posterior covariance matrix and computing matrix inverses, we add independent Gaussian noise to the encoded measurement 𝐲 z {\mathbf{y}}_{z} and the mean of the clean-latent prior. We then solve the resulting linear equations using conjugate gradients (CG) to obtain a corrected clean latent. For a linear operator, this basic construction gives an exact posterior sample when the equations are solved exactly. With the nonlinear learned network, the result is an approximate posterior sample, because we linearize the network locally and solve the equations with only a few CG iterations. The solver requires derivatives only through 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} , without back-propagating through the denoiser or decoder. The encoder and decoder are each used only once, to encode the degraded image 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} and decode the reconstruction. We make three contributions: 1 A back-propagation-free sampler for learned operators. We turn each denoising step into a Gaussian inference problem in latent space and sample it by perturbing and solving. For a linear operator and an exact solve, this sample is exact; for a nonlinear one, we linearize the operator locally, and the sample is approximate. This takes back-propagation-free latent updates beyond inpainting, to any degradation with a learned latent operator. 2 Fast and memory-efficient by design. The update needs only a few CG iterations through the small learned network ( ∼ \sim 1M parameters). It never back-propagates through the denoiser, never forms a Jacobian or covariance matrix, and runs the autoencoder only twice per reconstruction. 3 Strong reconstruction quality at lower cost. Across five restoration tasks on FFHQ and COCO, with a diffusion prior (RV-v5.1) and a flow prior (SD3.5), PASEO ranks first or second in LPIPS on almost every task. With SD3.5, it runs up to 19 × 19\times faster and uses up to 34 % {\color[rgb]{0.2266,0.5586,0.7578}34\%} less peak memory than the baselines, with the same or fewer denoiser evaluations.

Each diffusion step is conditioned on the measurement through a small learned operator 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} in latent space. Only 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} is differentiated, never the denoiser , and the autoencoder runs only once. Numbers match Steps 1–4 (Algorithm 3 ). We begin with the observation that equation 2.7 does not produce a Gaussian surrogate posterior transition that can be sampled in closed form when the degradation operator is a learned network 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} . PASEO uses the proxy construction from equation 2.7 , which avoids gradients through the denoiser, and extends it to equation 2.8 . This yields a Gaussian approximation to the surrogate posterior transition. We achieve this by (i) locally approximating the learned operator with a linear map, and (ii) using perturbations to sample the surrogate transition efficiently without forming or inverting its covariance matrix. Figure 2 gives an overview and Algorithm 3 the pseudocode. Training the latent operator. Before describing the sampler, we briefly explain how 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} is trained. Following Raphaeli et al. (2025) , we train a small network offline for each degradation and latent space to predict the encoded degraded measurement from the encoded clean image, minimizing an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} prediction loss. The diffusion model and autoencoder remain fixed, and 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} is kept fixed during sampling. Full training details are given in Appendix E.1 . 1 The denoiser only sets the prior. We now turn to sampling with the trained operator, which acts on clean latents; we denote them 𝐳 0 {\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}} and color them green . Written with the Woodbury identity ( Henderson & Searle, 1981 ) , its mean is 𝐦 p = 𝝁 z + K ⁡ ( 𝐲 z − H ​ 𝝁 z ) , K := η z 2 ​ H T ​ S − 1 , S := r 2 ​ 𝐈 d + η z 2 ​ H ​ H T {\mathbf{m}}_{p}={\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\bm{\mu}}_{z}}+{K}\big({\color[rgb]{0.8789,0.375,0.0625}{\mathbf{y}}_{z}}-{H}{\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\bm{\mu}}_{z}}\big),\qquad{K}:=\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}{S}^{-1},\qquad{S}:=r^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}{H}^{T} (3.2) (Appendix A.2 ). For a general H {H} , S {S} couples all coordinates and the covariance 𝚺 p \mathbf{\Sigma}_{p} is a dense d × d d\times d matrix. A direct sample would take the form 𝐳 0 = 𝐦 p + 𝚺 p 1 / 2 ​ 𝝃 {\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}}={\mathbf{m}}_{p}+\mathbf{\Sigma}_{p}^{1/2}\bm{\xi} , with 𝝃 ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 d ) \bm{\xi}\sim\mathbf{N}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) , which needs this matrix and its square root; both are out of reach at latent sizes (with SD3.5, d = 65,536 d=65{,}536 , so 𝚺 p \mathbf{\Sigma}_{p} has about 4.3 4.3 billion entries). {\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+}} is an exact draw from 𝐍 ⁡ ( 𝐦 p , 𝚺 p ) \mathbf{N}({\mathbf{m}}_{p},\mathbf{\Sigma}_{p}) (Appendix A.4 ). This works because the formula is linear in its two inputs: noise that enters at the prior’s and the measurement’s levels leaves with exactly the posterior’s spread. The perturb-and-solve identity itself is known in the sampling literature ( Papandreou & Yuille, 2010 ; Bardsley et al., 2014 ) . Our observation is that, once the proxy fixes the noise prediction, conditioning a latent diffusion step reduces to exactly this problem; Step 3 extends it to the learned operator by local linearization. Two consequences follow. A sample costs the same as the mean. The sample uses the same solve as the mean, only with the noisy inputs: S ​ 𝐯 = 𝐲 ~ z − H ​ 𝝁 ~ z {S}{\mathbf{v}}={\color[rgb]{0.8789,0.375,0.0625}\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}}-{H}{\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}} gives 𝐳 0 + = 𝝁 ~ z + η z 2 ​ H T ​ 𝐯 {\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+}}={\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}{\mathbf{v}} . The conjugate gradient (CG) method ( Hestenes & Stiefel, 1952 ) solves it using only products with H {H} and H T {H}^{T} , so neither S {S} nor 𝚺 p \mathbf{\Sigma}_{p} is ever built (Appendix A.3 ). The denoiser is never differentiated. It enters only through the fixed value 𝝁 z {\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\bm{\mu}}_{z}} . For a mask, equation 3.3 reduces to the closed-form step of equation 2.7 (Appendix D.1 ). 3 Solving with the learned operator. So far the operator was a fixed linear map. In practice it is the learned network 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} , and the forward degradation model becomes 𝐲 z = 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) + ϵ {\color[rgb]{0.8789,0.375,0.0625}{\mathbf{y}}_{z}}={\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\color[rgb]{0.1797,0.4883,0.1953}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}})+{\mathbf{\epsilon}} . The identity equation 3.3 needs a linear map, so we cannot apply it to 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} directly. sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Models and datasets. We evaluate PASEO on five degradation tasks: × 4 \times 4 and × 8 \times 8 super-resolution, Gaussian blur ( 61 × 61 61\times 61 , σ = 3 \sigma=3 ), 256 × 256 256\times 256 center inpainting, and JPEG decompression at quality 10 % 10\% , all at σ 𝐲 = 0.01 \sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}=0.01 . We use two latent priors: diffusion-based RV-v5.1 ( SG161222, 2023 ) and flow-based Stable Diffusion 3.5 (medium) ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . For sampler evaluation, we use 1000 1000 held-out FFHQ ( Karras et al., 2019 ) images and 1000 1000 COCO-val2017 ( Lin et al., 2014 ) images, all at 512 × 512 512\times 512 . Evaluation, metrics, and baselines. Following Raphaeli et al. (2025) , we train a separate latent degradation operator 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} for each task. For FFHQ, we split the dataset into 68,000 68{,}000 training, 1000 1000 validation, and 1000 1000 evaluation images. For COCO, we train on the 84,990 84{,}990 LSDIR-train images ( Li et al., 2023 ) , validate on 250 250 LSDIR validation images, and evaluate on the first 1000 1000 COCO-val2017 images. Appendix E.1 gives the training details. We report the following metrics: PSNR ( Horé & Ziou, 2010 ) and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , KID ( Bińkowski et al., 2018 ) for distributional alignment, wall-clock seconds per image and peak device memory in GiB. We emphasize LPIPS, since PSNR favors overly smooth images when exact recovery is impossible ( Janati et al., 2025 , App. B.6) . Across FFHQ and COCO, we compare PASEO against SILO , ReSample ( Song et al., 2024 ) , PSLD and GML-DPS ( Rout et al., 2023 ) , LDPS ( Chung et al., 2023 ) , DING , DAPS , RedDiff ( Mardani et al., 2024 ) , FlowDPS , FlowChef ( Patel et al., 2025 ) , and PnP-Flow . sections.heading: 4.1 Main results
sections.text: We report two versions of PASEO . Our analysis uses the original anchor of Algorithm 3 , a fresh draw from the prior. Early in sampling, however, the prior is wide, and this anchor can land far from the proxy’s clean latent. Our default, PASEO , therefore uses the arc anchor of equation 3.6 , which reuses part of the proxy noise to start near that latent. We also report PASEO † , which keeps the original anchor. FFHQ. With both priors, PASEO ranks first or second in LPIPS on almost every task, while running faster and with less memory than every baseline except the inpainting-only DING (Table 1 ). With RV-v5.1, the baselines are published results that use far more denoiser evaluations ( 999 999 NFEs for SILO , against our 53 53 ), yet PASEO or PASEO † has the lowest LPIPS on both super-resolution tasks and blur; SILO keeps inpainting and JPEG. With SD3.5, where every baseline gets more NFEs, PASEO has the best LPIPS on four of the five tasks (Appendix G ). Against the strongest baseline, ReSample , it is 10 10 – 20 × 20\times faster and uses about 25 % 25\% less memory; the price is PSNR, which is higher for ReSample on four tasks (Table 23 ). JPEG, our only nonlinear degradation, is the hardest case for our sampler with both priors. DING is faster on inpainting at the same memory, but it handles only that task, and with SD3.5 PASEO beats it on all three quality metrics. COCO. At matched NFEs, PASEO beats the flow-matching baselines FlowDPS , FlowChef , and PnP-Flow on every task in LPIPS, runtime, and memory (Table 4.2 ; reconstructions in Figure 1 ). Against all baselines (Table 25 ), PASEO or PASEO † still has the lowest LPIPS on every task except JPEG, which is again the hardest case. Across the 15 15 settings of Tables 1 and 4.2 , PASEO † beats PASEO in 3 3 and is within 0.02 0.02 LPIPS in 5 5 more, so the original anchor also works in practice. We keep the arc anchor as the default because it is better in the remaining cases and up to 7 × 7\times faster. Why JPEG is hard. Each correction relies on one question: if the latent changes slightly, how does the measurement change? For blur, super-resolution, and inpainting, the answer is smooth and reliable, because these degradations are linear. JPEG instead rounds the image’s frequency coefficients to fixed levels: small changes to the image leave the output unchanged, and the output changes only in abrupt jumps, when a coefficient crosses to the next level. There is no reliable local direction to follow, and the learned operator cannot supply one, so the corrections get little guidance. This makes JPEG our hardest case with both priors. We test this in Appendix E.2 , where the learned operator’s local directions for JPEG do not match those of the true degradation.

We also draw the ground truth from the model’s own prior, so that a calibrated sampler should see it as one more draw (Appendix F.1.2 ). sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Conditioning a latent diffusion model on a learned operator does not require back-propagating through the denoiser. PASEO casts each step as Gaussian inference over the clean latent, so conditioning becomes a perturb-and-solve step that is exact for affine operators, forms no Jacobian, and runs the autoencoder only twice per reconstruction; a few CG iterations beat an exact solve. Across FFHQ and COCO, with the same or fewer denoiser evaluations than every baseline, PASEO ranks first or second in LPIPS on almost every task, while running up to 19 × {\color[rgb]{0.2266,0.5586,0.7578}19\times} faster and using up to 34 % {\color[rgb]{0.2266,0.5586,0.7578}34\%} less peak memory than the baselines. Limitations. PASEO needs a trained latent operator for each degradation–prior pair, and its quality is bounded by that operator: on JPEG, where the learned operator’s local directions are poorest, PASEO is weakest.

sections.text: Let 𝐝 := 𝐲 − H ​ 𝝁 z {\mathbf{d}}:={\mathbf{y}}-{H}{\bm{\mu}}_{z} and S := σ 𝐲 2 ​ 𝐈 d 𝐲 + η z 2 ​ H ​ H T {S}:=\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d_{{\mathbf{y}}}}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}{H}^{T} . sections.heading: Derivation.
sections.text: From Appendix A.2 , 𝐦 p = 𝝁 z + η z 2 ​ H T ​ S − 1 ​ 𝐝 {\mathbf{m}}_{p}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}{S}^{-1}{\mathbf{d}} . For every nonzero 𝐮 {\mathbf{u}} and σ 𝐲 > 0 \sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}>0 , 𝐮 T ​ S ​ 𝐮 = σ 𝐲 2 ​ ‖ 𝐮 ‖ 2 + η z 2 ​ ‖ H T ​ 𝐮 ‖ 2 > 0 , {\mathbf{u}}^{T}{S}{\mathbf{u}}=\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}^{2}\|{\mathbf{u}}\|^{2}+\eta_{z}^{2}\|{H}^{T}{\mathbf{u}}\|^{2}>0, because the first term is strictly positive. The extreme eigenvalues satisfy λ min ​ ( S ) ≥ σ 𝐲 2 , λ max ​ ( S ) = σ 𝐲 2 + η z 2 ​ ‖ H ‖ 2 2 . \lambda_{\min}({S})\geq\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}^{2},\qquad\lambda_{\max}({S})=\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}^{2}+\eta_{z}^{2}\|{H}\|_{2}^{2}. sections.heading: A.4 Posterior sampling by input perturbation
sections.text: The solve above produces the posterior mean, whereas a posterior draw would seem to require a square root of 𝚺 p \mathbf{\Sigma}_{p} . Instead, randomness can be introduced through the Gaussian prior and likelihood before applying the same measurement-space solve.

sections.heading: Result.
sections.text: Draw independent 𝝃 z ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 d ) \bm{\xi}_{z}\sim\mathbf{N}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) and 𝝃 y ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 d 𝐲 ) \bm{\xi}_{y}\sim\mathbf{N}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d_{{\mathbf{y}}}}) , and set 𝝁 ~ z := 𝝁 z + η z ​ 𝝃 z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}:={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}\bm{\xi}_{z} and 𝐲 ~ := 𝐲 + σ 𝐲 ​ 𝝃 y \tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}:={\mathbf{y}}+\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}\bm{\xi}_{y} . With S := σ 𝐲 2 ​ 𝐈 d 𝐲 + η z 2 ​ H ​ H T {S}:=\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d_{{\mathbf{y}}}}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}{H}^{T} , solve and update S ​ 𝐯 = 𝐲 ~ − H ​ 𝝁 ~ z , 𝐳 0 + = 𝝁 ~ z + η z 2 ​ H T ​ 𝐯 . {S}{\mathbf{v}}=\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}-{H}\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z},\qquad{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+}=\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}{\mathbf{v}}. For a fixed linear model and an exact solve, the central distributional claim is 𝐳 0 + ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 𝐦 p , 𝚺 p ) . \boxed{{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+}\sim\mathbf{N}({\mathbf{m}}_{p},\mathbf{\Sigma}_{p}).} (A.4) Here 𝐦 p = 𝝁 z + η z 2 ​ H T ​ S − 1 ​ ( 𝐲 − H ​ 𝝁 z ) , 𝚺 p = η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d − η z 4 ​ H T ​ S − 1 ​ H . {\mathbf{m}}_{p}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}{S}^{-1}({\mathbf{y}}-{H}{\bm{\mu}}_{z}),\qquad\mathbf{\Sigma}_{p}=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\eta_{z}^{4}{H}^{T}{S}^{-1}{H}. The randomized solve replaces the deterministic mean solve; it is not an additional solve.

sections.heading: Derivation.
sections.text: Let K = η z 2 ​ H T ​ S − 1 {K}=\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}{S}^{-1} . Substituting the perturbed inputs into the gain-form update gives 𝐳 0 + \displaystyle{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+} = 𝝁 ~ z + K ⁡ ( 𝐲 ~ − H ​ 𝝁 ~ z ) \displaystyle=\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}+{K}(\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}-{H}\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}) = 𝝁 z + K ⁡ ( 𝐲 − H ​ 𝝁 z ) ⏟ = 𝐦 p + η z ​ ( 𝐈 d − K ​ H ) ​ 𝝃 z + σ 𝐲 ​ K ​ 𝝃 y . \displaystyle=\underbrace{{\bm{\mu}}_{z}+{K}({\mathbf{y}}-{H}{\bm{\mu}}_{z})}_{=\,{\mathbf{m}}_{p}}+\eta_{z}({\mathbf{I}}_{d}-{K}{H})\bm{\xi}_{z}+\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}{K}\bm{\xi}_{y}. This is an affine function of two independent Gaussian vectors and is therefore Gaussian. Since both perturbations have zero mean, 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐳 0 + ] = 𝐦 p \mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+}]={\mathbf{m}}_{p} . Independence also makes the cross-covariance terms vanish, giving Cov ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 + ) = η z 2 ​ ( 𝐈 d − K ​ H ) ​ ( 𝐈 d − K ​ H ) T + σ 𝐲 2 ​ K ​ K T . \operatorname{Cov}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+})=\eta_{z}^{2}({\mathbf{I}}_{d}-{K}{H})({\mathbf{I}}_{d}-{K}{H})^{T}+\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}^{2}{K}{K}^{T}. Because S {S} is symmetric, K ​ H {K}{H} is symmetric. Expanding the covariance and using the definition of S {S} yields Cov ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 + ) \displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+}) = η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d − 2 ​ η z 2 ​ K ​ H + K ⁡ ( η z 2 ​ H ​ H T + σ 𝐲 2 ​ 𝐈 d 𝐲 ) ​ K T \displaystyle=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-2\eta_{z}^{2}{K}{H}+{K}\bigl(\eta_{z}^{2}{H}{H}^{T}+\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d_{{\mathbf{y}}}}\bigr){K}^{T} = η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d − 2 ​ η z 2 ​ K ​ H + K ​ S ​ K T . \displaystyle=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-2\eta_{z}^{2}{K}{H}+{K}{S}{K}^{T}. The identity K ​ S = η z 2 ​ H T {K}{S}=\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T} implies K ​ S ​ K T = η z 2 ​ K ​ H {K}{S}{K}^{T}=\eta_{z}^{2}{K}{H} . Hence Cov ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 + ) = η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d − η z 2 ​ K ​ H = η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d − η z 4 ​ H T ​ S − 1 ​ H = 𝚺 p . \operatorname{Cov}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{+})=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\eta_{z}^{2}{K}{H}=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\eta_{z}^{4}{H}^{T}{S}^{-1}{H}=\mathbf{\Sigma}_{p}. Together with the mean calculation, this proves the distributional statement in equation A.4 . Equivalently, the two perturbations provide the rectangular covariance factor [ η z ​ ( 𝐈 d − K ​ H ) | σ 𝐲 ​ K ] , \left[\;\eta_{z}({\mathbf{I}}_{d}-{K}{H})\;\middle|\;\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}{K}\;\right], whose product with its transpose is 𝚺 p \mathbf{\Sigma}_{p} . A symmetric square root is therefore unnecessary. This exactness result assumes the fixed linear model above and an exact linear solve. Truncated CG, damping, or relinearization yields an approximate draw, as in the practical nonlinear update of Algorithm 3 . Appendix F.1.1 checks this result numerically.

sections.heading: Appendix B Nonlinear learned-operator extension
sections.text: The preceding derivations assume a fixed linear measurement map. We now derive the local linear model used when that map is the nonlinear learned operator 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} .

sections.heading: B.1 Local linearization of the learned operator
sections.text: At one inner update, the DDIM bridge supplies the clean-latent belief 𝐳 0 ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 𝝁 z , η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}\sim\mathbf{N}({\bm{\mu}}_{z},\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) , while the encoded observation obeys 𝐲 z = 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) + ϵ {\mathbf{y}}_{z}={\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{0})+{\mathbf{\epsilon}} with ϵ ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 0 , r 2 ​ 𝐈 d ) {\mathbf{\epsilon}}\sim\mathbf{N}(0,r^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) . The only part that prevents the linear–Gaussian analysis above is the nonlinearity of 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} . At a fixed expansion point 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} , let 𝐡 j := 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) {\mathbf{h}}_{j}:={\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}) and 𝐉 j := ∂ 𝐇 ψ / ∂ 𝐳 0 | 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{J}}_{j}:=\left.\partial{\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}/\partial{\mathbf{z}}_{0}\right|_{{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}} .

sections.text: The central approximation is the first-order linearization 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) ≈ 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) . \boxed{{\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{0})\approx{\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}).} (B.1) Moving the known affine offset to the measurement side defines 𝐲 eff ( j ) := 𝐲 z − 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)}:={\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} , for which 𝐲 eff ( j ) \displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)} ≈ 𝐉 j ​ 𝐳 0 + ϵ , \displaystyle\approx{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}+{\mathbf{\epsilon}}, 𝐲 eff ( j ) − 𝐉 j ​ 𝝁 z \displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\bm{\mu}}_{z} = 𝐲 z − 𝐡 j − 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝝁 z − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) . \displaystyle={\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}({\bm{\mu}}_{z}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}). Thus the nonlinear likelihood is locally the same linear–Gaussian model as before, with H {H} replaced by 𝐉 j {\mathbf{J}}_{j} and 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} by 𝐲 eff ( j ) {\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)} .

sections.heading: Derivation.
sections.text: Taylor’s theorem writes the operator as 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) = 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) + 𝐑 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) , {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{0})={\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)})+\mathbf{R}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}), where 𝐑 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) \mathbf{R}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}) is the remainder. If the Jacobian is L L -Lipschitz on the line segment joining 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} and 𝐳 0 {\mathbf{z}}_{0} , then ‖ 𝐑 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) ‖ ≤ L 2 ​ ‖ 𝐳 0 − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ‖ 2 . \|\mathbf{R}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0})\|\leq\frac{L}{2}\|{\mathbf{z}}_{0}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}\|^{2}. Substituting the expansion into the observation model and moving the known affine offset gives 𝐲 z \displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}_{z} = 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) + 𝐑 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) + ϵ \displaystyle={\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)})+\mathbf{R}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0})+{\mathbf{\epsilon}} 𝐲 z − 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ 𝐳 0 ( j ) \displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} = 𝐉 j ​ 𝐳 0 + 𝐑 j ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) + ϵ . \displaystyle={\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}+\mathbf{R}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{0})+{\mathbf{\epsilon}}. After the remainder is discarded, this is the claimed linear–Gaussian model. Its residual at the Gaussian-prior center is 𝐲 eff ( j ) − 𝐉 j ​ 𝝁 z \displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\bm{\mu}}_{z} = 𝐲 z − 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ 𝐳 0 ( j ) − 𝐉 j ​ 𝝁 z \displaystyle={\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\bm{\mu}}_{z} = 𝐲 z − 𝐡 j − 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝝁 z − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) , \displaystyle={\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}({\bm{\mu}}_{z}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}), as stated above. sections.heading: B.2 Perturb-and-solve sampling for a fixed local model
sections.text: Fix 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} independently of the perturbations used below, and write 𝐡 j := 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) {\mathbf{h}}_{j}:={\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}) and 𝐉 j := ∂ 𝐇 ψ / ∂ 𝐳 0 | 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{J}}_{j}:=\left.\partial{\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}/\partial{\mathbf{z}}_{0}\right|_{{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}} . sections.heading: Result.
sections.text: When the following local system is solved exactly, the update is an exact draw from the fixed affine-surrogate posterior: S j ​ 𝐯 = 𝐲 ~ z − 𝐡 j − 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝝁 ~ z − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) , 𝐳 0 ⋆ = 𝝁 ~ z + η z 2 ​ 𝐉 j T ​ 𝐯 , 𝐳 0 ⋆ ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 𝐦 j , 𝚺 j ) . \boxed{\begin{aligned} {S}_{j}{\mathbf{v}}&=\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}(\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}),\\ {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{\star}&=\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}+\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{J}}_{j}^{T}{\mathbf{v}},&{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{\star}&\sim\mathbf{N}({\mathbf{m}}_{j},\mathbf{\Sigma}_{j}).\end{aligned}} (B.2)

sections.heading: Derivation.
sections.text: The fixed affine surrogate is 𝐳 0 ∼ 𝐍 ( 𝝁 z , η z 2 𝐈 d ) , 𝐲 eff ( j ) ∣ 𝐳 0 ∼ 𝐍 ( 𝐉 j 𝐳 0 , r 2 𝐈 d ) . {\mathbf{z}}_{0}\sim\mathbf{N}({\bm{\mu}}_{z},\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}),\qquad{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)}\mid{\mathbf{z}}_{0}\sim\mathbf{N}({\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0},r^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}). Applying Appendices A.2 and A.4 to this fixed affine model requires only the substitution ( 𝐲 , σ 𝐲 , H ) ⟼ ( 𝐲 eff ( j ) , r , 𝐉 j ) . ({\mathbf{y}},\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}},{H})\longmapsto({\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)},r,{\mathbf{J}}_{j}). Under this substitution, those results give the moments above. In particular, the unperturbed residual is 𝐲 eff ( j ) − 𝐉 j ​ 𝝁 z \displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\bm{\mu}}_{z} = 𝐲 z − 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ 𝐳 0 ( j ) − 𝐉 j ​ 𝝁 z \displaystyle={\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\bm{\mu}}_{z} = 𝐲 z − 𝐡 j − 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝝁 z − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) = 𝐝 j . \displaystyle={\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}({\bm{\mu}}_{z}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)})={\mathbf{d}}_{j}. For sampling, perturb the prior center and the original measurement before forming the effective measurement: 𝐲 ~ eff ( j ) := 𝐲 ~ z − 𝐡 j + 𝐉 j ​ 𝐳 0 ( j ) . \tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(j)}:=\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}+{\mathbf{J}}_{j}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)}. The Jacobian is still evaluated at 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} . To verify the distribution of the output, let K j := η z 2 ​ 𝐉 j T ​ S j − 1 {K}_{j}:=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{J}}_{j}^{T}{S}_{j}^{-1} . Substituting the two perturbed inputs into the local update gives 𝐳 0 ⋆ \displaystyle{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{\star} = 𝝁 ~ z + K j ​ ( 𝐲 ~ z − 𝐡 j − 𝐉 j ​ ( 𝝁 ~ z − 𝐳 0 ( j ) ) ) \displaystyle=\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}+{K}_{j}\bigl(\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{h}}_{j}-{\mathbf{J}}_{j}(\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)})\bigr) = 𝝁 z + K j ​ 𝐝 j ⏟ = 𝐦 j + η z ​ ( 𝐈 d − K j ​ 𝐉 j ) ​ 𝝃 z + r ​ K j ​ 𝝃 y . \displaystyle=\underbrace{{\bm{\mu}}_{z}+{K}_{j}{\mathbf{d}}_{j}}_{=\,{\mathbf{m}}_{j}}+\eta_{z}({\mathbf{I}}_{d}-{K}_{j}{\mathbf{J}}_{j})\bm{\xi}_{z}+r{K}_{j}\bm{\xi}_{y}. Therefore Cov ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 ⋆ ) = η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d − η z 2 ​ K j ​ 𝐉 j = η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d − η z 4 ​ 𝐉 j T ​ S j − 1 ​ 𝐉 j = 𝚺 j , \operatorname{Cov}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{\star})=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\eta_{z}^{2}{K}_{j}{\mathbf{J}}_{j}=\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\eta_{z}^{4}{\mathbf{J}}_{j}^{T}{S}_{j}^{-1}{\mathbf{J}}_{j}=\mathbf{\Sigma}_{j}, which proves equation B.2 . sections.heading: B.3 Jacobian-free conjugate gradients

sections.heading: Appendix C Anchor construction and analysis
sections.text: Section 3 introduced the interpolated anchor in equation 3.6 : it replaces the perturbed-prior mean 𝝁 ~ z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z} in Algorithm 3 ’s measurement correction by interpolating toward the denoiser’s clean estimate. This appendix explains that construction and derives its statistical effect on the first correction.

sections.heading: C.1 Why interpolate the anchor?
sections.text: Early in sampling, the clean latent is inferred from a highly noisy state, and its Gaussian belief is broad: η z = η t / α t \eta_{z}=\eta_{t}/\alpha_{t} is large. A fresh draw 𝝁 ~ z = 𝝁 z + η z ​ 𝝃 z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}\bm{\xi}_{z} can therefore lie far from the denoiser’s clean estimate, where we linearize the learned operator. The measurement correction must then account for a large displacement before it can refine the reconstruction. This is demanding for the short CG solves used in our sampler. The interpolation in equation 3.6 reduces this displacement by favoring the denoiser’s estimate while the belief is broad. As the belief narrows, it returns to the original perturbed-prior anchor. This trades some of the ideal update’s conditional variability for a correction that is easier to compute with a small solver budget; the anchor ablation in Appendix F.2 measures the reconstruction consequences. Why the distance can be large. The denoiser’s estimate can be written as 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) = 𝝁 z + η z ​ 𝐰 ′ {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime} ; we derive this identity in the next subsection. Here 𝐰 ′ {\mathbf{w}}^{\prime} is the bridge noise already used to construct the clean-latent belief. The original anchor 𝝁 ~ z = 𝝁 z + η z ​ 𝝃 z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}\bm{\xi}_{z} instead uses independent fresh noise 𝝃 z \bm{\xi}_{z} . Subtracting gives 𝝁 ~ z − 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) = η z ​ ( 𝝃 z − 𝐰 ′ ) . \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}=\eta_{z}(\bm{\xi}_{z}-{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime}). Each coordinate of these independent standard Gaussian noises has variance 1 1 , so their difference has variance 1 + 1 = 2 1+1=2 . Summing over the d d latent coordinates and averaging over both noise draws gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝝁 ~ z − 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ‖ 2 ] = η z 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 d 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( ξ z , i − w i ′ ) 2 ] = 2 ​ d ​ η z 2 . \mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}\|^{2}\right]=\eta_{z}^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\xi_{z,i}-w^{\prime}_{i})^{2}\right]=2d\,\eta_{z}^{2}. The root-mean-square distance is therefore 2 ​ d ​ η z \sqrt{2d}\,\eta_{z} : the broader the belief, the larger the gap. For illustration, the SD3.5 SR × 8 \times 8 configuration uses a reverse-diffusion schedule with 100 100 timesteps. Across its anchor updates, η z \eta_{z} falls from about 250 250 to 0.03 0.03 . These timesteps describe progress from noise toward the reconstructed image; they are separate from the CG iterations used to solve each local correction. How the anchor enters the correction. Let 𝐳 a {\mathbf{z}}_{a} denote the replacement anchor: the value substituted for 𝝁 ~ z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z} in Algorithm 3 ’s residual and proposal. We write 𝝁 ~ z new := 𝐳 a \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}^{\mathrm{new}}:={\mathbf{z}}_{a} , while reserving 𝝁 ~ z = 𝝁 z + η z ​ 𝝃 z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}\bm{\xi}_{z} for the original perturbed-prior anchor. The algorithm keeps its general form; the anchor choice changes these two occurrences of its input. The learned operator 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} predicts a measurement from a clean latent. To compute a correction, we approximate this operator near the denoiser’s estimate 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)} by a linear model. Its Jacobian 𝐉 0 {\mathbf{J}}_{0} describes how the predicted measurement changes when the latent moves. At the replacement anchor, this model predicts 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 a ) ≈ 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ) + 𝐉 0 ​ ( 𝐳 a − 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ) . {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{a})\approx{\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)})+{\mathbf{J}}_{0}({\mathbf{z}}_{a}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}). Thus moving from the denoiser’s estimate to the anchor also changes the predicted measurement. Subtracting this prediction from the perturbed measurement target 𝐲 ~ z \tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z} used in Algorithm 3 gives 𝐲 ~ z − 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ) ⏟ mismatch at the denoiser’s estimate − 𝐉 0 ​ ( 𝐳 a − 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ) ⏟ predicted change from moving to the anchor . \underbrace{\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)})}_{\text{mismatch at the denoiser's estimate}}\;-\;\underbrace{{\mathbf{J}}_{0}({\mathbf{z}}_{a}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)})}_{\text{predicted change from moving to the anchor}}. This is the right-hand side of the linear system in equation 3.5 . The second term is the extrapolation term : it accounts for using an anchor away from the point where the local model was built. Why the limited solve matters. Conjugate gradients (CG) approximately solves that linear system. We allow at most three iterations per solve ( C ≤ 3 C\leq 3 ), so the computed correction need not satisfy the equation exactly. The relative CG residual measures the remaining error in that equation, divided by the norm of its right-hand side. Its mean value on SR × 8 \times 8 is 0.69 0.69 , indicating that the solves are far from converged. The resulting correction error can leave noise for the next denoiser call to remove. Why interpolation helps. Moving the anchor toward the denoiser’s estimate reduces their separation and the associated change in the linear model’s prediction. At the denoiser endpoint, 𝐳 a = 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) {\mathbf{z}}_{a}={\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)} , the extrapolation term above is zero. The correction then starts with the measurement mismatch at the denoiser’s estimate alone. This is the computational motivation for favoring that endpoint when the belief is broad.

sections.text: Recovering the denoiser endpoint. We first derive the identity used above. Fix one diffusion transition and omit its index. Evaluating the denoiser at this proxy gives a clean estimate 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) = 𝐱 ^ 0 θ ​ ( 𝐱 pxy , t ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}=\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{pxy}},t) and a noise estimate 𝐱 ^ 1 ′ = 𝐱 ^ 1 θ ​ ( 𝐱 pxy , t ) \hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{1}^{\prime}=\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{1}^{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{pxy}},t) . These are two ways of expressing the same prediction: the clean and noise components recombine into the input, 𝐱 pxy = α t ​ 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) + σ t ​ 𝐱 ^ 1 ′ . {\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{pxy}}=\alpha_{t}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}+\sigma_{t}\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{1}^{\prime}. Here α t \alpha_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} are the signal and noise coefficients of the diffusion schedule. For the flow-matching parameterization, α t + σ t = 1 \alpha_{t}+\sigma_{t}=1 and both estimates are affine in one velocity evaluation. The clean-latent belief in equation 3.1 is defined by 𝝁 z = 𝐦 − σ t ​ 𝐱 ^ 1 ′ α t , η z = η t α t . {\bm{\mu}}_{z}=\frac{{\mathbf{m}}-\sigma_{t}\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{1}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{t}},\qquad\eta_{z}=\frac{\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}. Substituting the bridge sample into the recombination identity and dividing by α t \alpha_{t} therefore gives 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) = 𝝁 z + η z ​ 𝐰 ′ . \boxed{\;{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime}.\;} (C.1) This explains the two endpoints: the denoiser’s estimate uses the bridge noise already involved in constructing the belief, while the original perturbed-prior anchor uses a fresh, independent draw. Mixing the two noise contributions. The coefficient c 1 c_{1} controls how much bridge noise we reuse, and c 2 c_{2} controls how much fresh noise we add. The mixing parameter β ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \beta\in[0,1] sets the balance between the denoiser’s estimate ( β = 0 \beta=0 ) and the original perturbed-prior anchor ( β = 1 \beta=1 ), as in equation 3.6 . At the first inner step, the anchor is 𝐳 a = 𝝁 z + η z ​ ( c 1 ​ 𝐰 ′ + c 2 ​ 𝝃 z ) , ( c 1 , c 2 ) = ( 1 − β 2 , β ) . {\mathbf{z}}_{a}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}(c_{1}{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime}+c_{2}\bm{\xi}_{z}),\qquad(c_{1},c_{2})=\big(\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}},\beta\big). sections.text: Within one diffusion transition, the sampler can apply several local corrections. Let j j count these inner corrections and 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} be the current estimate. After each correction, the next local model is built at the updated estimate, and the anchor is recomputed using that estimate in place of the initial denoiser output. The same original perturbed-prior draw is reused throughout. (C.6) The quantities 𝝁 z {\bm{\mu}}_{z} , 𝝁 ~ z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z} , 𝐲 ~ z \tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z} , η z \eta_{z} and β \beta stay fixed within the transition, while 𝐳 0 ( j ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(j)} and its local linearization change. The first-step calculation treated the denoiser’s estimate as fixed and independent of the two fresh perturbations. After a correction, the current estimate already contains effects of those same perturbations, 𝝃 z \bm{\xi}_{z} and 𝝃 y \bm{\xi}_{y} . At β = 0 \beta=0 the anchor is the current iterate; at β = 1 \beta=1 it is the fixed perturbed prior mean 𝝁 ~ z \tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z} on every inner step. For a fixed affine operator 𝐇 ψ ​ ( 𝐳 ) = H ​ 𝐳 + 𝐛 {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}({\mathbf{z}})={H}{\mathbf{z}}+{\mathbf{b}} , the latter choice gives the same residual 𝐲 ~ z − H ​ 𝝁 ~ z − 𝐛 \tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}-{H}\tilde{{\bm{\mu}}}_{z}-{\mathbf{b}} at every linearization. With λ = 0 \lambda=0 , ρ = 1 \rho=1 , the unweighted likelihood, and exact solves, the first correction is the affine posterior draw and every later correction returns that same draw: P = 1 P=1 suffices but is not necessary. sections.heading: D.1 Exact special cases of the measurement step
sections.text: This section relates the measurement step of Section 3 (Step 3; the ideal measurement update underlying Algorithm 3 ) to four published samplers. The step is a linear–Gaussian posterior update taken from an anchor in the clean-latent space, and it is determined by three choices: the anchor from which the update is taken, the ratio η z 2 / r 2 \eta_{z}^{2}/r^{2} that weights the measurement against the prior, and the solver that applies the resulting gain. Fixing these three choices recovers the measurement steps of DDS ( Chung et al., 2024a ) , of DiffPIR ( Zhu et al., 2023 ) for a linear operator, of DDNM ( Wang et al., 2023 ) with the Moore–Penrose inverse, and of DING ( Moufad et al., 2026 ) in distribution. Each subsection states the published update and reduces it to ours in four steps. Exactness is understood in exact arithmetic under the stated idealization: the reductions identify the point the step converges to, not the iterate a truncated solver returns. The reductions concern the measurement step only: recovering a method’s step does not recover its outer sampling loop. Two further methods that match the step only to first order are treated in Appendix D.2 .

sections.heading: The PASEO measurement step.
sections.text: Consider one sampling step. The clean-latent prior is 𝐍 ⁡ ( 𝝁 z , η z 2 ​ 𝐈 d ) \mathbf{N}({\bm{\mu}}_{z},\eta_{z}^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) , the measurement model is 𝐲 z = H ​ 𝐳 0 + ϵ {\mathbf{y}}_{z}={H}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}+{\mathbf{\epsilon}} with ϵ ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 0 , r 2 ​ 𝐈 d ) {\mathbf{\epsilon}}\sim\mathbf{N}(0,r^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) , and S = r 2 ​ 𝐈 d + η z 2 ​ H ​ H T {S}=r^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}{H}^{T} and K = η z 2 ​ H T ​ S − 1 {K}=\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}{S}^{-1} are as in Section 3 . Starting from an anchor 𝐳 a {\mathbf{z}}_{a} , the measurement step is 𝐳 0 ⋆ = 𝐳 a + K ⁡ ( 𝐲 ~ z − H ​ 𝐳 a ) , 𝐲 ~ z = 𝐲 z + r ​ 𝝃 y , {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{\star}={\mathbf{z}}_{a}+{K}\big(\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}-{H}{\mathbf{z}}_{a}\big),\qquad\tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z}={\mathbf{y}}_{z}+r\bm{\xi}_{y}, (D.1) where 𝐲 ~ z \tilde{{\mathbf{y}}}_{z} is the measurement perturbed by its own noise. The anchor is one of two points. It is either the denoised estimate 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) {\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)} , or the prior mean perturbed by its own noise, 𝝁 z + η z ​ 𝝃 z {\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}\bm{\xi}_{z} . With the second anchor, equation D.1 is an exact draw from the posterior when the solve is exact (Appendix A.4 ); with the first, it is a correction of the denoised estimate, deterministic when the measurement is not perturbed. DDS, DiffPIR and DDNM are compared in the simplest setting: a linear operator H {H} , a single iteration, no mask or damping, the anchor at the denoised estimate, and no measurement perturbation. DING keeps the second anchor and the perturbation, and is compared with equation D.1 directly. Under the simplest setting equation D.1 becomes 𝐳 0 ⋆ = 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) + η z 2 ​ H T ​ ( r 2 ​ 𝐈 d + η z 2 ​ H ​ H T ) − 1 ​ ( 𝐲 z − H ​ 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ) , \boxed{\;{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{\star}={\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}^{T}\big(r^{2}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}+\eta_{z}^{2}{H}{H}^{T}\big)^{-1}\big({\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{H}{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}\big),\;} (D.2) which is the minimiser of 1 2 ​ r 2 ​ ‖ 𝐲 z − H ​ 𝐳 ‖ 2 + 1 2 ​ η z 2 ​ ‖ 𝐳 − 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ‖ 2 \frac{1}{2r^{2}}\big\|{\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{H}{\mathbf{z}}\big\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2\eta_{z}^{2}}\big\|{\mathbf{z}}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}\big\|^{2} (D.3) (Appendix A.2 ). Scaling equation D.3 by η z 2 \eta_{z}^{2} does not change its minimiser and gives τ 2 ​ ‖ 𝐲 z − H ​ 𝐳 ‖ 2 + 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐳 − 𝐳 0 ( 0 ) ‖ 2 , τ = η z 2 r 2 , \frac{\tau}{2}\big\|{\mathbf{y}}_{z}-{H}{\mathbf{z}}\big\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\big\|{\mathbf{z}}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{(0)}\big\|^{2},\qquad\tau=\frac{\eta_{z}^{2}}{r^{2}}, (D.4) so only the ratio τ \tau matters: it sets how far the measurement is allowed to move the denoised estimate. sections.heading: D.2 First-order special cases of the measurement step
sections.text: Two published samplers, FlowChef ( Patel et al., 2025 ) and PnP-Flow ( Martin et al., 2025 ) , apply the measurement as a single gradient step on the data misfit rather than as a solve. Neither is an exact special case of equation D.2 ; both are its first-order truncation, and the term they discard is exactly the one our solver computes. This section states that truncation once and then reduces each method to it. The notation and the simplest setting of Appendix D.1 apply throughout.

sections.heading: E.1 Latent-operator training details
sections.text: We follow the recipe of Raphaeli et al. (2025) , training one operator per degradation and per latent space, offline. For a clean image 𝐱 {\mathbf{x}} , we form a measurement as in equation 2.3 with 𝐧 ∼ 𝐍 ⁡ ( 0 , s 2 ​ 𝐈 ) {\mathbf{n}}\sim\mathbf{N}(0,s^{2}{\mathbf{I}}) and s ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.04 ) s\sim\mathcal{U}(0,0.04) , resample it to the encoder’s resolution, and minimize the loss ℒ ⁡ ( ψ ) = 𝔼 𝐱 , s , 𝐧 ​ ‖ 𝐇 ψ ​ ( ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) , s ) − ℰ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) + 𝐧 ) ‖ 1 . \mathcal{L}(\psi)=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}},s,{\mathbf{n}}}\big\|\,{\mathbf{H}}_{\psi}\big({\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{x}}),s\big)-{\mathcal{E}}\big({\mathcal{A}}({\mathbf{x}})+{\mathbf{n}}\big)\big\|_{1}. (E.1) Conditioning on s s lets one operator serve a range of noise levels; at sampling time we pass the known σ 𝐲 \sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}} . 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} is a 1.2 1.2 M-parameter CNN used in Raphaeli et al. (2025) acting at latent resolution, so a forward pass and a Jacobian–vector product cost far less than one denoiser evaluation. We use FFHQ- 512 512 with the evaluation images held out, Adam with a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and a batch size of 16 16 ; the prior and autoencoder stay frozen, and the operator never sees a diffusion state. Its nonlinearity is load-bearing: ℰ ∘ 𝒜 ∘ 𝒟 {\mathcal{E}}\circ{\mathcal{A}}\circ{\mathcal{D}} is nonlinear even for linear 𝒜 {\mathcal{A}} , and a matched affine operator fits the latent measurement 4.8 4.8 – 8.1 8.1 dB worse on super-resolution. Appendix E.2 compares the trained operator’s values and Jacobian with those of the true chain.

sections.heading: E.2 Validation of the learned operator and its Jacobian
sections.text: A useful learned operator must predict both the encoded measurement and how that measurement changes when the latent moves. Table 5 checks these separately against the true decode–degrade–encode chain. The saved reconstructions use the arc anchor; inpainting uses the hard mask rather than the learned weighting of the main results (Appendix F.6.1 ). Prediction and direction. Panel A compares clean-image latents with re-encoded saved reconstructions. Value error often exceeds the noise scale r r assumed by the solver: for RV-v5.1 blur, the RMS error is 0.31 0.31 against r = 0.005 r=0.005 . This comparison does not validate r r as a calibrated error model. On the four non-JPEG tasks, direction agreement on clean latents is higher for SD3.5 (cosine 0.87 0.87 – 0.96 0.96 ) than RV-v5.1 ( 0.37 0.37 – 0.63 0.63 ). Errors on re-encoded reconstructions are not uniformly smaller; SD3.5 super-resolution is a counterexample. JPEG needs particular care because the reference derivative itself is sensitive to the finite-difference step. Numerical consistency. Panel B asks whether the forward and transpose Jacobian products agree and estimates a condition-number bound. The small adjoint discrepancies support the consistency of those two implemented products. They do not establish that the learned Jacobian is accurate, or that the CG solve converges. Likewise, a large estimated bound suggests potential numerical difficulty but is not a measurement of the actual condition number. Table 5: Does the learned operator predict both measurements and their local changes? Eight test images and four random directions per image and configuration. sections.heading: E.3 Metric protocol
sections.text: KID is reported relative to the task, not on an absolute scale: the observations handed to the sampler score 65.68 65.68 , 176.31 176.31 , 46.39 46.39 , 117.64 117.64 , and 42.90 42.90 for SR × 4 \times 4 , SR × 8 \times 8 , Gaussian blur, center inpainting, and JPEG, respectively, so a larger reconstruction KID on SR × 8 \times 8 than on SR × 4 \times 4 reflects how far the measurement starts from the data distribution, not a worse reconstruction. KID is therefore comparable within a task and across methods, and not across tasks. Memory is the peak allocated memory reported by PyTorch, which is measured per process and is unaffected by co-tenancy.

sections.heading: Appendix F Ablations and diagnostics
sections.text: We examine the practical sampler through four questions: whether it matches the posterior when that posterior is known, how the anchor and solver settings affect reconstruction, how computation is allocated, and what changes specifically in inpainting. The learned operator is validated separately alongside its training details in Appendix E.2 .

sections.heading: F.1 Checking the sampler against known posteriors
sections.text: We check the sampler on two problems whose posterior is known. The first is a small linear–Gaussian problem that tests the ideal update of Appendix A.4 . The second runs the full SD3.5 sampler with exact linear operators in place of the learned one.

sections.heading: F.1.1 A linear–Gaussian problem
sections.text: Table 8 checks whether the update in equation A.4 produces the right distribution, including its uncertainty. We use a linear–Gaussian problem whose posterior mean and covariance are known exactly, and ask three questions. 1. Does the ideal update work? An exact solve reproduces the posterior mean, covariance and interval coverage up to sampling error. This provides a numerical check of the derivation. 2. What changes when we approximate the update? Stopping conjugate gradients (CG) after one or two iterations shifts the sample mean and distorts the covariance. By C = 8 C=8 iterations, this 32 32 -dimensional linear solve matches the exact-solve reference. Taking only a fraction ρ < 1 \rho<1 of the correction also shifts the mean and makes the samples too spread out. 3. What does changing the anchor do? Here the distinction is whether we redraw the bridge noise 𝐰 ′ {\mathbf{w}}^{\prime} for each sample or keep it fixed. With fresh bridge noise, every tested β \beta recovers the posterior in this affine experiment. With fixed bridge noise, as in repeated updates from one bridge state, β < 1 \beta<1 shifts the center and narrows the distribution: β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 retains about 57 % 57\% of the posterior spread, and β = 0 \beta=0 about 30 % 30\% . Appendix C derives this shift in equation C.3 and the variance change. Averaging coverage over different fixed bridge noises can still give about 90 % 90\% , so coverage alone does not reveal this mismatch. These checks concern the affine update; they do not establish exact posterior sampling for the full nonlinear algorithm. Table 8: Checking samples against a known Gaussian posterior. sections.heading: F.1.2 The full sampler with exact linear operators
sections.text: The image experiments run a different algorithm: a learned operator, a few CG iterations, and the arc anchor. Table 9 checks this full SD3.5 sampler on problems whose posterior is known. We keep the sampler and replace the learned operator 𝐇 ψ {\mathbf{H}}_{\psi} with an exactly linear operator in latent space. Every linearization is then exact, so any departure from the posterior comes from the solver, the anchor, or the diffusion prior, not from operator error. We ask three questions. Setup. Both operators act on the 16 × 64 × 64 16\times 64\times 64 SD3.5 latent of a 512 × 512 512\times 512 image. The random-hole mask 𝐇𝐳 = 𝐌 ⊙ 𝐳 {\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{z}}={\mathbf{M}}\odot{\mathbf{z}} hides 20 % 20\% of the latent cells in 16 × 16 16\times 16 -pixel holes aligned to the latent grid (Figure 5 ). The circular latent blur blurs each channel with a Gaussian of one latent cell ( 8 8 pixels); it is diagonal in the Fourier basis, so the local system of Appendix A.3 can be solved exactly at every step. Each image has one measurement 𝐲 = 𝐇𝐳 ⋆ + r ​ 𝝃 {\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{H}}{\mathbf{z}}^{\star}+r\bm{\xi} with r = 0.01 r=0.01 . A calibration test needs a truth that is itself a posterior draw, so we draw 𝐳 ⋆ {\mathbf{z}}^{\star} from the model’s own prior by running the sampler with nothing observed; we also report real FFHQ faces, passed through the same final denoiser step as the draws. The sampler is SD3.5-medium with 28 28 steps, P = 1 P=1 , ρ = 1 \rho=1 , and λ = 0 \lambda=0 . We compare three anchors (Appendix C ): the perturbed prior ( β = 1 \beta=1 ), the arc, and the denoiser anchor ( β = 0 \beta=0 ). Each draws 20 20 samples per image, with shared measurements and seeds, so the differences are paired. Checks. If the sampler is correct, the truth behaves like one more draw. The spread ratio S S divides the RMS distance between draws by the RMS distance from the draws to the truth; S = 1 S=1 when calibrated, and below 1 1 means the draws vary too little or are off-center. Unlike the spread in Table 8 , it compares the draws with the truth. The rank of the truth among the 20 20 draws is uniform when calibrated; TV is the distance of its histogram from uniform. Both look at one coordinate at a time and can miss structured errors, so we also divide the energy of the draws in each Fourier band by that of the truth; 1 1 is the right amount of detail. Intervals are 95 % 95\% bootstrap intervals over images. The mask and the main blur comparison use 100 100 images; the CG sweep uses 64 64 . Does the sampler match the posterior when the update is exact? With a coordinate mask, one CG iteration solves the linear system exactly, so PASEO with β = 1 \beta=1 takes the same closed-form step as DING (Appendix D.1.4 ). Block 1 of Table 9 confirms that the two agree, to within ± 0.001 \pm 0.001 in spread. Every sampler is within 3 % 3\% of calibrated (spread 1.02 1.02 – 1.03 1.03 ), and the rank histograms are nearly flat (Figure 7 a). The small excess is shared with DING , so it comes from the 28 28 -step discretization and the final denoiser step, not from the measurement update. The anchors barely differ, because the correction is zero inside the holes; the mask tests the outer loop, and the blur tests the anchor and the solver. With real faces, every sampler, DING included, reads about 1.08 1.08 , because the SD3.5 prior is broader than FFHQ. The last column is the per-pixel standard deviation over 20 20 draws: the variation sits in the holes. 2. What changes when we solve exactly instead of stopping CG early? The blur couples neighboring cells, so the solver now matters (Table 9 , block 2). The exact solve adds a mesh-like texture (Figure 6 ): its LPIPS is 0.73 0.73 – 0.78 0.78 , against 0.06 0.06 – 0.07 0.07 with C = 5 C=5 CG iterations, and real faces show the same. The spread ratio misses this, since the texture changes from draw to draw, but the band energies show it (Table 10 ): in the finest band, where the blur keeps 1 % 1\% of the signal, the exact solve has 15 15 – 19 19 times the energy of the truth, and C = 5 C=5 has 0.9 0.9 – 1.2 1.2 . The cause is the per-step prior. Early in sampling η z \eta_{z} is large, so the exact update fits even the directions that the blur almost erases and amplifies the noise in them; the isotropic per-step Gaussian does not know that natural latents carry little energy there. CG started from zero fits the strongly observed directions first, so a few iterations leave the rest to the diffusion prior. This does not contradict Appendix F.1.1 , where the exact solve is the reference: there the per-step Gaussian is the true prior, so fitting every direction is correct. sections.heading: F.2.1 Anchors at the same solver budget
sections.text: The anchor is the latent from which the measurement correction is taken (Section 3 , Appendix C ). Early in sampling, the original perturbed-prior anchor can lie far from the denoiser’s estimate. Table 11 asks how the choice between these anchors affects reconstruction when the solver budget is held fixed. Defining the five anchors. Here 𝝁 z {\bm{\mu}}_{z} and η z \eta_{z} are the center and standard deviation of the clean-latent belief, 𝐰 ′ {\mathbf{w}}^{\prime} is the bridge noise already used by the denoiser, and 𝝃 z \bm{\xi}_{z} is an independent standard Gaussian draw. All five choices can therefore be written as 𝐳 a = 𝝁 z + η z ​ ( c 1 ​ 𝐰 ′ + c 2 ​ 𝝃 z ) . {\mathbf{z}}_{a}={\bm{\mu}}_{z}+\eta_{z}(c_{1}{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime}+c_{2}\bm{\xi}_{z}). The coefficients c 1 c_{1} and c 2 c_{2} specify how much bridge noise we reuse and how much fresh noise we add. sections.text: The practical sampler requires choices about how many corrections to make, how accurately to solve each linear system, and how far to move at each correction. Reporting results at selected settings does not show how much reconstruction quality depends on these choices. This section identifies which settings need careful tuning and which have little effect over the tested range, helping readers understand the sensitivity of the reported performance. sections.heading: F.4 Computational budget and reconstruction quality
sections.text: To assess the sampler’s efficiency, we need to understand what extra computation buys in reconstruction quality. We can take more reverse sampling steps, apply more measurement corrections within each step, or allow more iterations to solve each correction. These choices increase the work in different ways, so we examine where additional computation helps and how much the limited solver leaves unresolved. We denote the number of reverse steps by K K , the number of measurement corrections per step by P P , and the maximum CG iterations per correction by C C . We first measure how changing K K affects quality and runtime. We then check how closely the solutions returned by the limited CG solver satisfy their linear equations. Both diagnostics use the arc anchor. Each experiment starts from the reference settings for its task and prior. All inpainting runs here use the supplied hard mask, whereas the main results use learned weights (Appendix F.6.1 ).

More steps consistently take more time, but their quality benefit depends on the task and metric. The 28 28 -step schedule is competitive on most tasks. For SD3.5, 56 56 steps improves LPIPS on inpainting and JPEG, while blur ties at the displayed precision. PSNR can improve even when LPIPS worsens. sections.heading: F.4.2 Accuracy of the truncated CG solves
sections.text: Reconstruction scores alone do not tell us how accurately the sampler solves its internal linear systems. This matters because the ideal update assumes an exact solve, while the practical sampler limits the number of CG iterations. We therefore measure the error remaining in the linear equations when CG stops. Table 16 summarizes these errors, and Figure 9 shows how they vary over the sampling steps. Reading the residuals. For a system with matrix S j {S}_{j} and right-hand side 𝐛 {\mathbf{b}} , let 𝐯 {\mathbf{v}} be the solution returned by CG. Its relative residual is ‖ S j ​ 𝐯 − 𝐛 ‖ ‖ 𝐛 ‖ . \frac{\|{S}_{j}{\mathbf{v}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|}{\|{\mathbf{b}}\|}. This measures the remaining error in the equation relative to the size of its right-hand side. Zero means an exact solve; 1 1 is the residual at the zero initial solution, and 0.5 0.5 means half that initial residual. A value above 1 1 means that the residual is larger than at initialization. The table reports the mean, median, and fraction of solves with relative residual above 0.5 0.5 . The logged-solve counts use k k for thousands. These summaries combine solves from the parameter sweeps, grouping them by prior and CG budget. Most groups have mean ratios above 1 1 . The RV-v5.1 C = 12 C=12 and SD3.5 C = 5 C=5 groups have much smaller means, 0.07 0.07 and 0.03 0.03 ; these budgets are used for inpainting. However, the recorded groups lack task identifiers and contain different mixtures of tasks and settings. Comparing their rows or the curves in Figure 9 therefore cannot isolate what increasing C C does to one fixed problem. A small mean also does not imply that every solve converged. The practical solves often fall short of the exact-solve assumption in equation 3.5 . The conditioning estimates in Table 5 suggest potential numerical difficulty, without establishing its cause. These measurements concern the linear equations; the separate sensitivity experiment in Appendix F.3 measures the quality of the final images. sections.heading: F.5 Repeatability and sample variation
sections.text: The reconstruction pipeline uses random draws, so repeating an evaluation can change both its average scores and individual reconstructions. We examine variation across eight seeded runs. In the newly rerun inpainting configurations, measurement construction is held fixed and only the sampling seed changes; the retained non-inpainting results use the legacy joint-seed protocol described below. This experiment uses the arc anchor and the reference settings for each task and prior. Its two inpainting rows use the mask-free soft likelihood weights from the main inpainting results; these weights are examined in Appendix F.6.1 .

sections.heading: F.5.1 Variation across repeated seeded reconstructions
sections.text: Similar average scores can hide differences between reconstructions of the same input or between repeated runs of the full stochastic pipeline. Here we examine how much the outputs vary, where that variation occurs, and how closely they agree with the reference measurement after degradation. For each of the first 50 50 test images, the two inpainting configurations construct the measurement with seed 0 0 and reconstruct it with eight sampling seeds ( 10 10 – 17 17 ). These rows therefore isolate reconstruction variation and use the current mask-free soft likelihood weighting configuration. The retained SR, blur, and JPEG rows use the legacy joint-seed protocol, in which the run seed affects both measurement construction and sampling; their statistics describe end-to-end repeatability and mix the two sources of randomness. Table 17 summarizes the results, and Figure 10 shows four runs for selected inputs. Where the images vary. Panel A summarizes three aspects of variation. Pixel standard deviation (std.) measures how much each pixel changes across the eight seeded runs, then averages over pixels and test images. Pixels are measured on the [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] scale. For inpainting, the parentheses report the hole and visible region separately; variation inside the hole is about 9 9 – 20 20 times larger. LPIPS mean and standard deviation describe quality and its variation across runs for each image, then average these quantities over images. The RMS distance ratio compares the mean pairwise distance between reconstructions with their mean reconstruction error to the reference image, using root mean square (RMS) distance for both. sections.heading: F.6 Inpainting case study
sections.text: Inpainting is the task for which the main results and the preceding ablations use different measurement weights: the main results use learned weights, while the ablations use a supplied mask. We examine how this choice affects reconstruction quality, whether its effect depends on the anchor, and which image regions account for the differences between anchors.

sections.heading: F.6.1 Supplied mask versus learned likelihood weighting
sections.text: The missing region contains no observed image content and should therefore be excluded from the measurement constraint. A supplied hard mask identifies this region explicitly. The learned weighting rule instead uses the operator’s sensitivity to determine which measurement coordinates receive weight, without receiving the mask. To measure the effect of this choice, we first compare the two rules with the arc anchor fixed in Table 18 . This comparison explains the quality and runtime consequences of the mask-free configuration used in the main results. How the learned weights are obtained. At each inner correction, we estimate how strongly each predicted measurement coordinate responds to a change in the latent. Coordinates with greater sensitivity receive larger weights in the likelihood. With J J denoting the local operator Jacobian, this gives w i ∝ ( J ​ J ⊤ ) i ​ i w_{i}\propto\sqrt{(JJ^{\top})_{ii}} , the norm of its i i th row. We estimate these quantities using four random probes, known as Hutchinson probes, without forming the Jacobian. The table calls this rule “learned weight”; we also refer to it as the soft weight below. What changes when the mask is withheld. On FFHQ with RV-v5.1, the soft weight improves PSNR, hole LPIPS and KID relative to the hard mask, while whole-image LPIPS worsens by 0.003 0.003 and runtime increases by about 25 % 25\% . With SD3.5, PSNR and both LPIPS scores are similar, while KID increases by about 0.7 0.7 . On COCO, the soft weight loses 0.12 0.12 dB PSNR, adds 0.008 0.008 LPIPS and increases KID by about 4.3 4.3 . Thus the cost of avoiding a supplied mask depends on the dataset and prior. The main tables report the mask-free rule consistently, including where the supplied mask performs better.

sections.heading: F.6.2 Interaction between anchor and weighting
sections.text: The learned weights are estimated during each correction, so their effect may depend on the anchor used for that correction. We therefore extend the comparison in Table 18 to the original perturbed-prior anchor, testing whether the weighting rule used with the arc also works well with this anchor. We also examine a rule that estimates the weights once and keeps them fixed throughout sampling. The perturbed-prior (“exact”) anchor corresponds to β = 1 \beta=1 in equation 3.6 and adds the full fresh prior perturbation, whereas the arc reduces that perturbation early in sampling. On RV-v5.1, combining the perturbed-prior anchor with the per-correction soft weight gives LPIPS 0.247 0.247 , compared with 0.139 0.139 when that anchor receives the hard mask. One possible explanation is that the stronger perturbation changes the operator’s sensitivity inside the hole, making the estimated weights less useful for excluding missing content. The table measures the resulting quality difference but does not isolate this mechanism. To test another weighting rule, we estimate the weights once at the encoded measurement and keep them fixed. We remove weights below 0.2 0.2 times the largest weight and shrink the retained region by one latent cell along its boundary. The table calls this thresholded and eroded rule “fixed weight.” For the RV-v5.1 perturbed-prior anchor, this rule improves LPIPS from 0.247 0.247 to 0.147 0.147 ; for the arc, it worsens LPIPS relative to the per-correction soft weight under both priors. Among the reported RV-v5.1 combinations, the denoiser anchor with the hard mask has the best quality scores and shortest runtime. The perturbed-prior anchor with the mask has the second-best quality scores. The arc variants have KID around 10 10 points above the denoiser-plus-mask result across the three tested weighting rules. The next experiment examines where this image-quality difference occurs. Reading the quality metrics. Table 18 reports LPIPS for both the whole image and the 256 × 256 256\times 256 missing region (the hole). KID compares the reconstructions with the paired reference images and is reported multiplied by 10 3 10^{3} . Higher PSNR and lower LPIPS and KID indicate better scores; runtime is measured in seconds per image. sections.heading: F.6.3 Where the reconstruction differences occur
sections.text: The denoiser and arc anchors produce different whole-image scores, but these scores do not show whether the difference lies in the filled hole or the visible background. We separate these regions to locate the quality gap. Table 19 compares both anchors on the same 1000 1000 test images under RV-v5.1, with the hard mask in both runs. In addition to scoring complete images and hole crops, we replace one region at a time with reference pixels so that only errors in the other region remain. Isolating the regions. Replacing the reconstructed hole with the reference hole leaves only background errors; both KID estimates then become close to zero. Conversely, inserting the reconstructed hole into the reference background leaves only errors inside the hole. This largely reproduces the whole-image gap: KID is 2.89 2.89 for the denoiser anchor and 17.31 17.31 for the arc, compared with 3.50 3.50 and 16.26 16.26 for the complete reconstructions. The difference therefore comes mainly from the filled region. Compare anchors within each row: cropping changes the input to the feature extractor, so crop scores and complete-image scores are not directly comparable. FID provides a complementary comparison. Interpreting the metrics. LPIPS compares each reconstruction with its own reference, whereas KID compares distributions of image features across the dataset. Repeated texture artifacts, visible in Figure 11 , can therefore produce a distributional gap while having a smaller effect on the average paired-image distance. This interpretation is consistent with the measurements; the regional experiment locates the gap without identifying the mechanism that causes the artifacts. Evaluation details. The regional comparison uses paired reference images, a 256 × 256 256\times 256 hole, and torchmetrics 1.5.2 1.5.2 with a KID subset size of 999 999 . KID is reported multiplied by 10 3 10^{3} . Small negative KID estimates can arise from the unbiased finite-sample estimator and do not establish that the two distributions are identical. The table highlights numerical differences, without testing their statistical significance. sections.heading: G.3 PSLD
sections.text: We followed the setup in SILO ’s Appendix D: PSLD uses its official repository with Stable Diffusion at 512 × 512 512\times 512 . We checked our PSLD implementation numerically against the released code; it agreed with it to within the repeat-to-repeat floor ( ≤ 2 × 10 − 7 \leq 2\times 10^{-7} absolute, cosine 1.0 1.0 ). Of the baselines in Table 1 , PSLD is the only one whose update needs the operator adjoint: its gluing term evaluates A ⊤ ​ y A^{\top}y and A ⊤ ​ A ​ D ​ ( z ) A^{\top}AD(z) explicitly, so an adjoint has to exist as a linear map. GML-DPS , LDPS and ReSample only apply H H and differentiate through it, which a nonlinear operator supports, so they run on every task. JPEG compression quantises transform coefficients, and quantisation is not linear, so there is no adjoint to supply: the obstruction is in the method–operator pair, not in our implementation of either. Substituting a plausible surrogate such as the identity would let PSLD run to completion while enforcing a different constraint, so we report the cell as unsupported instead. Raphaeli et al. (2025) report no PSLD entry for this task either, so the left block’s cell is “n/a” as well. PSLD ’s memory on Gaussian blur is higher because it is the only sampler that needs the operator adjoint: the exact adjoint of the 61 × 61 61\times 61 blur kernel is an autograd vector–Jacobian product whose double-backward graph costs a further 2.1 2.1 GiB under both priors, so that cell is reported on its own. What separates the two groups is the gluing term, which puts the encoder in the graph: PSLD sits at 7.87 7.87 GiB on its three remaining tasks and GML-DPS at 7.89 7.89 GiB, while ReSample and LDPS backpropagate through the decoder alone at 6.97 6.97 GiB – a cost of 0.90 0.90 and 0.92 0.92 GiB respectively.

sections.heading: G.6 DING
sections.text: DING ( Moufad et al., 2026 ) is the method Section 3 builds on, and the only row of Table 1 needing neither a trained operator nor a denoiser Jacobian. For a coordinate mask, its measurement step is an exact special case of ours (Appendix D.1.4 ). Two choices behind that row affect the reported results, and neither is forced by the algorithm.

sections.heading: G.6.1 DING : carrying a pixel mask into the latent
sections.text: DING ’s update is closed-form because its measurement enters as a coordinate mask on the clean latent: the resulting conditional is Gaussian with a diagonal covariance. Our benchmark instead measures in pixels, 𝐲 = 𝐌 pix ⊙ 𝐱 + σ 𝐲 ​ 𝐧 {\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{M}}_{\mathrm{pix}}\odot{\mathbf{x}}+\sigma_{{\mathbf{y}}}{\mathbf{n}} , so the mask has to be carried into the latent, and there are two ways to do it. Encode the reference, then mask: 𝐌 ⊙ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) {\mathbf{M}}\odot{\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{x}}) . This is what a latent inpainting task yields by default and what the released code constructs. It is inadmissible on a pixel-measurement benchmark. ℰ {\mathcal{E}} has a receptive field wider than one latent cell, so a cell just outside the hole is computed partly from pixels inside it; because ℰ {\mathcal{E}} is applied to the true image, those border cells carry the hidden content. A sampler pinned to them as observed reads part of the fill it is meant to infer. Restricted to the visible cells the two observations differ by 6.4 % 6.4\% in relative ℓ 1 \ell_{1} under SD3.5 and 14.2 % 14.2\% under RV-v5.1, with maximum per-cell deviations of 1.24 1.24 and 2.16 2.16 . Encode the measurement, then mask: 𝐌 ⊙ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐲 ) {\mathbf{M}}\odot{\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{y}}) . This is what we use. It cannot leak, because 𝐲 {\mathbf{y}} contains nothing inside the hole, and it is the only construction under which DING and our sampler receive the same information. We verify that the pixel observation DING is handed is identical, entry for entry, to our own sampler’s on every image.

sections.heading: G.6.2 What that choice costs DING
sections.text: The adaptation is not neutral, and we would rather state its cost than claim it is. DING ’s conjugacy assumes the observation is the clean latent restricted to the visible cells. Under 𝐌 ⊙ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐲 ) {\mathbf{M}}\odot{\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{y}}) the cells adjacent to the hole are not: they encode a blank region, so they differ from the corresponding entries of ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) {\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{x}}) by the same receptive-field effect that makes the other construction inadmissible. DING is therefore pinned to slightly incorrect values in a one-cell ring around the hole. This is a model misspecification we impose; on DING ’s own benchmark the measurement is latent by definition, 𝐌 ⊙ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) {\mathbf{M}}\odot{\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{x}}) is not leakage there, and no such mismatch arises. The reported row is consequently a measurement of DING on our problem and is not comparable to the authors’ published results. We do not have a measurement isolating the size of this effect. The check reported below — that the visible region is reconstructed at the autoencoder’s ceiling, 29.57 29.57 dB with the four-channel latent and 34.29 34.29 dB with the sixteen-channel one — establishes that the coordinate mask is honoured rather than approximated, but it is an average over the whole visible region and a one-cell ring at the boundary would be swamped by the interior. It should not be read as evidence that the boundary is unaffected. A third construction would remove both problems: erode the latent mask by one cell, so that the ambiguous border cells enter neither the observation nor the leakage path. It costs a small number of observed cells and would leave DING with an exactly specified, non-leaking measurement. We did not run it, and we flag it as the fairer comparison rather than presenting 𝐌 ⊙ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐲 ) {\mathbf{M}}\odot{\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{y}}) as the last word. We report 𝐌 ⊙ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐲 ) {\mathbf{M}}\odot{\mathcal{E}}({\mathbf{y}}) because between the two constructions we did evaluate, it is the only one that gives every method the same information; the alternative would hand DING an advantage no other method receives.

sections.heading: G.6.3 Evaluation budget and regional metrics
sections.text: DING spends 2 ​ ( n − 2 ) + 1 2(n-2)+1 denoiser evaluations at n n steps: two for each of its n − 2 n-2 iterations, plus a final clean-latent prediction. A batched classifier-free pair counts once. At n = 41 n=41 this is 79 79 , the baselines’ budget, a count confirmed by instrumenting the network rather than inferred from the step count. We report a single arm: the two-arm protocol of Appendix G.2 exists because a data-consistency step size chosen at one step count is detuned at another, and DING has no such parameter — its only knobs are the step count and the noise schedule η \eta . The argument is structural: DING exposes no data-consistency step size that could be detuned by a change of budget. What the row does not show. Whole-image metrics understate the task, since three quarters of the image is observed. Restricted to the 256 × 256 256\times 256 fill, DING attains 16.13 16.13 dB and 0.377 0.377 LPIPS under RV-v5.1 and 15.77 15.77 dB and 0.378 0.378 under SD3.5. The visible region is reconstructed at the autoencoder’s ceiling in both cases, 29.57 29.57 dB with the four-channel latent and 34.29 34.29 dB with the sixteen-channel one. This confirms that the coordinate mask is honored rather than approximated. All values are computed over the same 1000 1000 images as the rest of Table 1 ; all runs completed without failure under eight-way GPU contention.

sections.heading: G.7 FlowDPS
sections.text: In the COCO tables, FlowDPS ( Kim et al., 2025 ) takes three data-consistency iterations per step at one NFE per step. Tuned step size: 10 10 (SR and blur) and 60 60 (JPEG); the published default is 5 5 .

sections.heading: Matched 27-NFE comparison.
